content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a strategy to fit a continuous, differentiable signal representations parameterized by neural networks (SIREN) to videos by adding a constrain to satisfy the optical flow equation. The aim of the work is to exploit the improved SIREN representation of the video for video frame interpolation without suffering from the temporal discretization of the classical methods. Some qualitative and quantitative results are shown indicating that the strategy achieves state of the art results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
* An interesting idea is presented about using optical flow to fit SIREN for videos

Weaknesses
* It is known that the use of early linearization to formulate the optical flow equation is only valid under the assumption that the image changes linearly along the displacement (not the general case) and specially fail under large displacements, which are one of the most interesting cases on frame interpolation
* There are no details about how the Video Frame Interpolation is computed
* The method is totally dependent on the quality of the provided optical flow, both for fitting SIREN and to then compute the VFI
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: To the best of my knowledge, the idea of using optical flow to constrain SIREN is novel. The paper misses a Section to treat how VFI is performed, and more visual and numerical analysis of the improvement on SIREN to improve video representation and how them allow a better interpolation of video frames. Reproducibility is limited with the described details, and no code or videos were shared
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the idea of using optical flow to constrain SIREN sounds promising, the paper suffers from a lack of explanation on why this formulation of the optical flow was used to constrain SIREN, knowing its limitations, and how the claimed improvements yield to a better generation of interpolated frame on video. It would be good if the authors can include a comparison with different optical flow methods, a section dedicated on how the improved SIREN is used to get the interpolated video frames, and more visual results to compare with state of the art methods

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose an optical flow constraint loss for video-implicit neural representations. The main idea is to involve the optical flow constraint to the loss. They demonstrate the experimental comparisons and ablation study to validate their proposed approach.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The optical flow constraint is interesting in improving performance.

Ablation study in section 4.3 is just parameter tuning rather than the ablation study. The effectiveness of the optical flow constraint is to be validated. For example, simple temporal and spatial gradient constraints are closely related to the proposed algorithm. Those kinds of simple extensions are compared to ablation studies.

For implementation details, it is unclear how to set \delta x, \delta y, and \delta t. Those parameters are important for the proposed algorithm. However, the discussion related to those parameters is missed.

In the experiments section, the authors mentioned that the ground truth optical flow was estimated with the original resolution. It is unclear that the FPS of the video for the optical flow estimation. I guess the training data is half FPS, but the original FPS video might be used to optical flow estimation. If so, I don't think that is fair comparison.
For fair comparisons, the ground truth optical flow should be estimated with the same video data of training. 

It may be good to evaluate the optical flow estimated from generated video images.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The derivation of the optical flow constraint is reasonable, but it is exactly the same as the classical optical flow constraint. In that sense, the derivation itself is not technically novel. Involving the optical flow constraint in the loss is interesting.
content.summary_of_the_review: The optical flow constraint is interesting. But, implementation details are not good enough to reproduce the proposed algorithm. In addition, I don’t think the experimental comparisons are fair condition.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a learning-based method for video frame interpolation. Specifically, it utilizes the recent trend of implicit neural representation to learn a mapping function from (x, y, t) to (r, g, b). The authors propose a novel OF loss to regularize the training. Quantitative and visual results show that the proposed method can achieve comparable quality with state-of-the-art methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- Strength
  - Integrating implicit functions with frame interpolation is interesting and exciting. 
  - The proposed method achieves surprisingly good quantitative results against existing methods.

- Weaknesses
  - The authors do not convince me that using implicit representation or SIREN to tackle the task of video frame interpolation is an efficient way. What is the weakness of existing flow-based CNN methods? Additionally, the proposed method requires per-sequence training, which is not practical for real-time applications.
  - Fig. 3 is quite confusing. Why is the red curve (w/ OF loss) a straight line? Does that mean you will not apply \omega as the frequency in SIREN when using the OF loss?
  - The evaluation dataset: Why do not use the common dataset such as Vimeo-90K, UCF101, Middlebury for limited motion evaluation? And why do you not consider X4K as the large motion dataset? Also, why do the numbers for X4K so different from the numbers reported in the FILM paper? Do you use the same testing set?
  - The proposed method heavily relies on the pre-calculated optical flow as the OF loss seems to play an essential role in the training. Is there any analysis of the effect of the optical flow?
  - The visual comparisons are too limited. Only two examples are shown in Fig. 5, one of them even the failure case. The visualization of the interpolated video is essential for this task. The authors need to provide more visual comparisons to demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method over existing methods. Wildly the proposed method beats most of the existing techniques in Table 1. I am very curious about how the visualization reflects the quantitative evaluation.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-written. As mentioned in the weakness section, the main drawback of this paper is the lack of visual comparisons. The novelty seems to be adequate. However, I am not convinced that using implicit functions for frame interpolation is a better way than CNN-based methods. I strongly encourage the authors to promise that they will release the source code and pre-trained models for reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: I like using implicit representation to tackle the frame interpolation task. However, this paper lacks visual comparisons and proper evaluations. I lean toward rejecting this paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a INR method to achieve video frame interpolation with a strong condition on optical flow constraint equation.  In particular, the authors consider SIREN structure as a backbone of INR. They demonstrate their performance in VFI of limited motion range and large motion range, and claim that their algorithm is superior in limited motion range VFI.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper applied SIREN structures for video INR. Honestly, this is not novel compared with VideoINR[CVPR 22] and NeRV [NeurIPS 21]. They are different tasks but already showed that INR is effective in spatio-temporal representations. Also, the general performances in VideoINR and NeRV showed the best performance compared with SOTA algorithms. However, this paper is second best in Large-motion VFI and the qualitative results are not promising.


Also, their construction of loss related with optical flow constraint looks suboptimal. In Fig.1, their loss is built upon two different domains (gradient domain and pixel domain). It may cause domain inconsistency (such as mismatched information could be raised from each domain) In addition, without such loss construction, there is no noticeable novel thing.

My biggest concern on this work is qualitative results. Especially in Fig.5(a), there are severe artifacts such as banding effects in the proposed results, and it's not a publishable quality. I believe that such artifacts should be reduced to be public their algorithm.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The quality of writing and clarity is moderate. 
As I mentioned previously, I fill lacked novelty on this paper in general. Also, I have a big concern on their qualitative results.
Demonstrations of qualitative results are insufficient, too.
I didn't check the existence of their source code.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper demonstrated SIREN architecture in VFI and obtained relatively good numbers in limited motion range videos; however, qualitatively, their results have severe artifacts. Such artifacts are not appealed in baselines, so the method includes a part generating such artifacts. The novelty of this paper is also limited in terms of the similarity with previous articles (VideoINR, NeRV, INRvideo compression). The loss function combining pixel loss and optical flow constraints may be considered as a new approach, but still, there are rooms to improve this, and it's not fully convinced of optimality.

content.title: Optical Flow Regularization of Implicit Neural Representations for Video Frame Interpolation
content.TL;DR: We show that constraining the derivatives of video INR to satisfy the optical flow constraint equation allows to reach state of the art VFI on limited motion ranges without relying on additional training data.
content.abstract: Recent works have shown the ability of Implicit Neural Representations (INR) to carry meaningful representations of signal derivatives. In this work, we leverage this property to perform Video Frame Interpolation (VFI) by explicitly constraining the derivatives of the INR to satisfy the optical flow constraint equation. We achieve state of the art VFI on limited motion ranges using only a target video and its optical flow, without learning the interpolation operator from additional training data. We further show that constraining the INR derivatives not only allows to better interpolate intermediate frames but also improves the ability of narrow networks to fit the observed frames, which suggests potential applications to video compression and INR optimization.
